s1-48.ref: Reddy's The Essentials of Forensic Medicine and Toxicology
w: Correct. Following Nysten's rule, rigor in voluntary muscle appears first in the eyelids.
Lower limbs stiffen late in the sequence.
Fingers and toes are the last to stiffen.
The neck stiffens after the eyelids, face and jaw.
steps: Rigor follows a fixed order in voluntary muscles.
It starts in small muscles of the head.
The eyelids are first.
It spreads downward and leaves in the same order.
s1-48.mn: Nysten's order: 'Eyes, Face, Neck, Trunk, Arms, Legs, Toes'.

s1-49.ref: Reddy's The Essentials of Forensic Medicine and Toxicology
w: Correct. Hanging gives an oblique, incomplete mark above the thyroid cartilage.
A horizontal, continuous mark suggests ligature strangulation.
A mark at or below the thyroid cartilage suggests strangulation.
Tracheal ring fractures point to violent compression such as throttling.
steps: Look at direction, continuity and level of the mark.
Body weight pulls the noose up towards the knot, so the mark is oblique.
At the knot the noose lifts off, so the mark is incomplete.
Above the thyroid cartilage, oblique and incomplete = hanging.

s1-50.ref: Reddy's The Essentials of Forensic Medicine and Toxicology
w: Correct. Cholera is a classic cause of postmortem caloricity.
Massive haemorrhage leads to rapid cooling.
Cold-water drowning speeds cooling.
Congestive heart failure is not a classic cause.
steps: Caloricity needs excess heat production or continuing bacterial activity.
Cholera, septicaemia and tetanus fit.
Strychnine convulsions and heat stroke also fit.
Haemorrhage and cold water do the opposite.

s1-51.ref: Reddy's The Essentials of Forensic Medicine and Toxicology
w: Correct. Embedded powder grains cause tattooing, which marks close range.
Flame causes burning and singeing.
Smoke causes blackening, which can be wiped off.
Bullet grease causes a grease collar or abrasion collar, not tattooing.
steps: Each discharge product travels a different distance.
Flame travels shortest, then smoke, then powder grains.
Powder embedded in skin cannot be wiped off: tattooing.
Its presence means the shot was fired at close range.

s1-52.ref: Reddy's Forensic Medicine and Toxicology; Harrison's (toxic alcohols)
w: Correct. Fomepizole blocks alcohol dehydrogenase and stops toxic metabolites forming.
Naloxone reverses opioids.
Flumazenil reverses benzodiazepines.
N-acetylcysteine treats paracetamol poisoning.
steps: Methanol itself is not very toxic; its metabolites are.
Alcohol dehydrogenase starts the conversion.
Block it with fomepizole (or saturate it with ethanol).
Dialysis removes methanol and formate.

s1-53.ref: Reddy's The Essentials of Forensic Medicine and Toxicology
w: Correct. Arsenic causes Mees lines on the nails.
Lead causes Burton's lines on the gums and basophilic stippling.
Mercury causes erethism and acrodynia.
Copper causes blue-green vomitus and haemolysis.
steps: Transverse white nail lines = Mees lines.
They are classic for arsenic (thallium too).
Look for skin pigmentation and neuropathy.
Hair and nail analysis can confirm exposure months later.

s1-54.ref: Reddy's The Essentials of Forensic Medicine and Toxicology
w: Correct. Gustafson's method uses six regressive changes in adult teeth.
Wrist ossification is used for age in children and adolescents.
Skull suture fusion is a rough method for older adults.
Pubic symphysis changes are Todd's method.
steps: Gustafson = teeth.
It applies to adults after eruption is complete.
It scores six degenerative changes.
Root transparency is considered the most reliable.

s1-55.ref: Reddy's The Essentials of Forensic Medicine and Toxicology
w: Correct. Locard's principle: every contact leaves a trace.
Daubert standard governs admissibility of expert scientific evidence (US).
McNaughten rule is a legal test of insanity.
Durham rule is another (product) test of insanity.
steps: The phrase 'every contact leaves a trace' is a direct quote of the idea.
It is attributed to Edmond Locard.
It is the basis of trace evidence.
The other options relate to law and insanity.

s1-56.ref: Park's Textbook of Preventive and Social Medicine
w: Correct. Sensitivity = true positives / all who have the disease.
TN/(TN+FP) is specificity.
TP/(TP+FP) is positive predictive value.
TN/(TN+FN) is negative predictive value.
steps: Draw the 2×2 table.
Sensitivity looks only at the diseased column.
Of those diseased, what fraction tested positive?
a/(a+c) = TP/(TP+FN).
s1-56.mn: SnNout: Sensitive test, Negative result, rules disease out. SpPin: Specific test, Positive result, rules disease in.

s1-57.ref: Park's Textbook of Preventive and Social Medicine
w: Correct. Case-control studies compare odds of exposure, giving the odds ratio.
Relative risk needs incidence, which comes from cohort studies.
Attributable risk also needs incidence (cohort).
Incidence cannot be measured when you start with cases.
steps: The study starts with disease status: case-control.
You cannot calculate incidence in a case-control study.
So relative risk is not possible directly.
The odds ratio estimates it (well, when disease is rare).

s1-58.ref: Park's Textbook of Preventive and Social Medicine
w: Correct. Higher prevalence raises PPV.
Sensitivity is a fixed property of the test.
Specificity is also fixed.
NPV falls as prevalence rises.
steps: Separate test properties from population-dependent values.
Sensitivity and specificity belong to the test.
Predictive values depend on how common the disease is.
More disease means a positive result is more likely real: PPV rises.

s1-59.ref: Park's Textbook of Preventive and Social Medicine
w: Correct. Tetanus comes from soil spores, not from people, so herd immunity cannot help.
Measles spreads person to person, so herd immunity protects.
Diphtheria spreads person to person.
Polio spreads person to person.
steps: Herd immunity blocks chains of transmission between people.
Tetanus has no human chain: infection comes from the environment.
So vaccinating others gives no indirect protection.
Every person must be vaccinated individually.

s1-60.ref: Park's Textbook of Preventive and Social Medicine; MoHFW National Vitamin A prophylaxis guidance
w: Correct. 1 lakh IU orally at 9 months, with MR vaccine.
2 lakh IU is the dose from 12 months onwards, every 6 months.
50,000 IU is not the programme dose for this age.
Vitamin A is given orally, not intramuscularly, in the programme.
steps: The first dose comes at 9 months.
Infants get the half dose: 1 lakh IU.
From the second dose onwards it is 2 lakh IU every 6 months.
Nine doses in total by age 5.

s1-61.ref: Park's Textbook of Preventive and Social Medicine
w: Correct. Horrocks apparatus estimates bleaching powder needed (chlorine demand).
Water hardness is measured by titration methods.
Residual chlorine is measured by the orthotolidine (OT) test.
Bacterial contamination is assessed by coliform counts.
steps: Horrocks = how much bleaching powder.
It uses starch-iodide to show the colour change.
OT test then checks residual chlorine.
Target: 0.5 mg/L free chlorine after 1 hour.

s1-62.ref: Park's Textbook of Preventive and Social Medicine
w: Correct. The submerged part is the hidden, undiagnosed and subclinical disease.
Cases seen by clinicians are the visible tip.
Deaths are part of the visible picture.
Carriers are only one part of the submerged portion.
steps: The visible tip = diagnosed clinical cases.
Below the water lies the larger hidden burden.
That burden includes undiagnosed and subclinical cases.
Screening aims to uncover it.

s1-63.ref: Park's Textbook of Preventive and Social Medicine; MoHFW Immunisation Handbook
w: Correct. OPV is the most heat-sensitive routine vaccine.
Tetanus toxoid is heat-stable but freeze-sensitive.
Hepatitis B vaccine is freeze-sensitive.
Pentavalent vaccine is freeze-sensitive.
steps: Split vaccines into heat-sensitive and freeze-sensitive.
Heat-sensitive live vaccines: OPV tops the list.
Adsorbed (alum) vaccines are freeze-sensitive.
VVM shows heat exposure; the shake test shows freezing.

s1-64.ref: Dhingra's Diseases of Ear, Nose and Throat
w: Correct. Negative Rinne + Weber to the same ear = conductive loss in that ear.
Sensorineural loss would give a positive Rinne and Weber to the opposite (better) ear.
Right conductive loss would lateralise Weber to the right.
Normal hearing gives a positive Rinne and a central Weber.
steps: Rinne negative: bone conduction beats air conduction, so conductive loss.
Weber goes to the side of conductive loss.
Both point to the left ear.
Diagnosis: left conductive hearing loss.

s1-65.ref: Dhingra's Diseases of Ear, Nose and Throat
w: Correct. Little's area on the anteroinferior septum is the commonest bleeding site.
Woodruff's plexus is a posterior bleeding site in older adults.
The middle turbinate is not a common source.
The roof of the nose is rarely the source.
steps: Most nosebleeds are anterior.
Anterior septal vessels meet in Little's area.
It is exposed to dry air and nose-picking.
Posterior bleeds (Woodruff's) are rarer and more serious.

s1-66.ref: Dhingra's Diseases of Ear, Nose and Throat
w: Correct. Carhart notch is a dip in bone conduction at 2000 Hz.
500 Hz is not where the notch occurs.
A 4000 Hz notch is typical of noise-induced hearing loss.
8000 Hz is not typical of otosclerosis.
steps: Otosclerosis = conductive loss from stapes fixation.
The fixed stapes alters bone conduction mechanics.
This produces an apparent BC dip at 2 kHz.
It disappears after stapes surgery.

s1-67.ref: Dhingra's Diseases of Ear, Nose and Throat
w: Correct. Petrous apicitis involves the abducens nerve (lateral rectus palsy).
Facial palsy is a complication of otitis media but not part of Gradenigo triad.
Hoarseness relates to vagus/recurrent laryngeal nerve, not part of the triad.
Vertigo can occur with labyrinthitis but is not in the triad.
steps: Ear infection spreading to the petrous apex.
The abducens nerve passes through Dorello's canal there.
The trigeminal ganglion lies close by, causing pain.
Triad: discharge, pain, diplopia from lateral rectus palsy.

s1-68.ref: Dhingra's Diseases of Ear, Nose and Throat
w: Correct. Quinsy is a peritonsillar abscess.
Parapharyngeal abscess lies lateral to the superior constrictor, with neck swelling.
Retropharyngeal abscess lies behind the pharynx, often in young children.
Pus in tonsillar crypts is follicular tonsillitis.

k: Between tonsil capsule and superior constrictor

steps: Quinsy = peritonsillar abscess.
Pus sits outside the tonsil capsule.
It causes trismus and displaces the uvula.
Drain at the point of maximum bulge.

s1-69.ref: Dhingra's Diseases of Ear, Nose and Throat
w: Correct. Bezold abscess lies deep to the sternocleidomastoid.
Citelli abscess tracks along the posterior belly of digastric.
Luc abscess lies deep to temporalis via the external canal.
Zygomatic abscess lies over the zygoma.
steps: Pus breaks out of the mastoid tip.
The tip gives attachment to the SCM.
Pus tracking deep to SCM = Bezold.
Learn each abscess by its route.

s1-70.ref: Dhingra's Diseases of Ear, Nose and Throat; Scott-Brown's Otorhinolaryngology
w: Correct. JNA pushes the posterior antral wall forward: Holman-Miller sign.
Inverted papilloma arises on the lateral nasal wall, with unilateral mass and risk of malignancy.
Antrochoanal polyp is a smooth, pale polyp from the maxillary antrum extending to the choana.
Maxillary carcinoma destroys bone rather than bowing it.
steps: Bowing of the posterior maxillary wall = Holman-Miller sign.
It means a mass in the pterygopalatine fossa.
In a teenage boy with nosebleeds, that mass is JNA.
Do not biopsy: torrential bleeding risk.

s1-71.ref: Dhingra's Diseases of Ear, Nose and Throat; AAO-HNS Bell's palsy guideline
w: Correct. Oral steroids started within 72 hours improve recovery in Bell's palsy.
Surgical decompression is not first-line in Bell's palsy.
Antivirals alone are not recommended; they may be added to steroids.
Botulinum toxin is used later for synkinesis, not acute treatment.
steps: Sudden isolated LMN facial weakness = Bell's palsy.
Steroids reduce nerve swelling in the bony canal.
Start them within 72 hours.
Protect the eye from exposure keratitis.

s1-72.ref: Khurana's Comprehensive Ophthalmology; Parsons' Diseases of the Eye
w: Correct. Laser peripheral iridotomy relieves pupillary block and is definitive.
Trabeculectomy is for uncontrolled glaucoma, not the first step.
Long-term acetazolamide is not definitive and has side effects.
Atropine dilates the pupil and can worsen angle closure.
steps: First lower IOP medically.
The cause is pupillary block, so make a new path for aqueous.
Laser peripheral iridotomy does this.
Treat the fellow eye prophylactically.

w: Correct. CRAO: pale retina with a cherry-red spot.
CRVO gives a 'blood and thunder' fundus with haemorrhages.
Retinal detachment gives a grey, billowing retina and field loss.
Vitreous haemorrhage obscures the fundus view.
steps: Sudden painless visual loss: think vascular.
A white retina means arterial ischaemia.
The fovea stays red because choroid shows through.
So: central retinal artery occlusion.

w: Correct. Koeppe nodules at the pupillary margin indicate granulomatous uveitis.
Acute angle closure does not cause iris nodules.
Bacterial keratitis affects the cornea, not the iris margin.
Allergic conjunctivitis causes papillae, not iris nodules.
steps: Iris nodules mean granulomatous inflammation.
Koeppe = pupillary margin; Busacca = iris surface.
Add mutton-fat keratic precipitates.
Look for sarcoidosis, TB, syphilis.
s1-74.mn: 'Koeppe at the Kerb (margin), Busacca on the Body (surface)'.

s1-75.ref: Khurana's Comprehensive Ophthalmology; National Blindness and Visual Impairment Survey (India)
w: Correct. Cataract is the leading cause of blindness in India.
Uncorrected refractive error is the leading cause of visual impairment, not blindness.
Glaucoma is an important but smaller cause.
Corneal opacity is a smaller cause.
steps: Separate blindness from visual impairment.
Blindness: cataract leads.
Visual impairment: refractive error leads.
Both are largely curable.

w: Correct. The swinging flashlight test detects RAPD.
Cover-uncover test detects squint.
Schirmer test measures tear production.
Ishihara chart tests colour vision.

k: Pupils dilate when light moves to bad eye

steps: Swing the light between the eyes every 2-3 seconds.
In a normal eye both pupils constrict.
When light reaches the damaged eye, both pupils dilate.
That paradoxical dilation is RAPD.

s1-77.ref: Khurana's Comprehensive Ophthalmology; WHO trachoma grading
w: Correct. Herbert's pits are pathognomonic of trachoma.
Vernal keratoconjunctivitis gives cobblestone papillae and Horner-Trantas dots.
Adenoviral conjunctivitis gives follicles and preauricular nodes.
HSV keratitis gives dendritic ulcers.
steps: Pits at the limbus = healed limbal follicles.
Named Herbert's pits.
Only trachoma causes them.
Arlt's line is the tarsal scar.

w: Correct. Painful red eye, ciliary flush, small pupil, normal IOP = anterior uveitis.
Angle closure has a mid-dilated pupil and high IOP.
Conjunctivitis has superficial congestion, discharge and a normal pupil.
Subconjunctival haemorrhage is painless with normal vision.
steps: Check the pupil size first.
Small pupil + ciliary flush = iris inflammation.
Normal IOP excludes angle closure.
Treat with steroids and cycloplegics.

w: Correct. Snellen is tested at 6 metres.
3 metres is used only for some charts in small rooms (with mirrors).
1 metre is used for finger counting tests.
10 metres is not standard.
steps: At 6 m, light from the chart is almost parallel.
So accommodation is not needed.
Each letter subtends 5 minutes of arc.
Normal vision is 6/6.

s1-80.ref: Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine; ACC/AHA/HRS SVT guideline
w: Correct. Adenosine transiently blocks the AV node, terminating AV-nodal re-entry.
Amiodarone is not first-line for stable SVT.
Oral digoxin acts too slowly for acute termination.
Lignocaine is for ventricular arrhythmias.
steps: Regular narrow-complex tachycardia = SVT.
Patient stable, vagal manoeuvres failed.
Next: adenosine rapid IV push with flush.
Unstable patients need cardioversion.

w: Correct. Streptococcus pneumoniae is the most common cause of CAP.
Mycoplasma causes atypical pneumonia, common in young adults but not most common overall.
Klebsiella affects alcoholics and diabetics.
Staph aureus is classically post-influenza.
steps: CAP in adults: pneumococcus leads.
Typical picture: lobar consolidation, rusty sputum.
Atypicals are common but not the top cause.
Grade severity with CURB-65.

w: Correct. SIADH: euvolaemic hyponatraemia, concentrated urine, urine sodium >30.
Hypovolaemia with low urine sodium suggests extrarenal salt loss.
Hypernatraemia with dilute urine suggests diabetes insipidus.
Oedema with low urine sodium suggests heart failure or cirrhosis.
steps: Check volume status: euvolaemic.
Urine is inappropriately concentrated for a low serum osmolality.
Urine sodium stays high.
That combination is SIADH.

s1-83.ref: Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine; ADA Hyperglycaemic Crises consensus
w: Correct. Start with isotonic saline to restore volume.
Insulin before fluids can worsen shock and hypokalaemia.
Bicarbonate is only for severe acidosis (pH <6.9).
DKA needs IV therapy, not oral.
steps: DKA patients are severely dehydrated.
Volume first: isotonic saline.
Check potassium, then start insulin.
Add dextrose once glucose falls.

w: Correct. Ipsilateral motor and dorsal column loss, contralateral pain and temperature loss.
This reverses the sides.
Bilateral pain/temperature loss suggests central or anterior cord lesion.
Hemisection does not cause ipsilateral loss of all sensory modalities.

k: DC and CST cross in medulla

steps: Know where each tract crosses.
Dorsal columns and corticospinal cross in the medulla.
Spinothalamic fibres cross near entry level.
So a hemisection gives split-side findings.

s1-85.ref: Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine; ACR/EULAR RA criteria
w: Correct. Anti-CCP is the most specific test for RA.
Rheumatoid factor is less specific.
ANA is non-specific.
Anti-dsDNA is specific for SLE.
steps: Specificity question: which test is rarely positive outside RA?
Anti-CCP above 95% specificity.
RF occurs in many conditions.
Anti-CCP also predicts erosive disease.

s1-86.ref: Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine; Endocrine Society guideline on phaeochromocytoma
w: Correct. Plasma free metanephrines are the most sensitive screening test.
VMA is less sensitive.
Serum cortisol is for Cushing or Addison.
MIBG is for localisation after diagnosis.
steps: Biochemistry first, imaging second.
Metanephrines are produced continuously inside tumour cells.
So they catch episodic secretors.
Then localise with CT/MRI.

w: Correct. SAAG ≥1.1 indicates portal hypertension.
Peritoneal TB gives low SAAG.
Peritoneal carcinomatosis gives low SAAG.
Pancreatic ascites gives low SAAG.
steps: SAAG = serum albumin minus ascitic albumin.
High gradient means high hydrostatic pressure.
That means portal hypertension.
Low gradient means peritoneal disease.

s1-88.ref: Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery
w: Correct. 4 × 60 × 30 = 7200 mL/24 h; half (3600 mL) in the first 8 hours.
7200 mL is the whole 24-hour total.
2400 mL is too little.
4800 mL is not half of 7200.
steps: Calculate total: 4 × 60 × 30 = 7200 mL.
Half of it goes in the first 8 hours.
Count from time of burn, not arrival.

s1-89.ref: Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery
w: Correct. Charcot's triad: fever, jaundice, RUQ pain.
Hypotension is added in Reynolds' pentad.
Confusion is added in Reynolds' pentad.
A palpable gallbladder is linked to Courvoisier's law.
steps: Cholangitis = infected obstructed bile duct.
Triad: fever, jaundice, RUQ pain.
Add shock and confusion for Reynolds' pentad.
Treat with drainage (ERCP).

s1-90.ref: Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery; Robbins
w: Correct. Papillary carcinoma is the most common thyroid cancer.
Follicular carcinoma is second.
Medullary carcinoma is less common.
Anaplastic carcinoma is rare and aggressive.
steps: Rank thyroid cancers by frequency.
Papillary is clearly the most common.
It spreads by lymphatics.
Prognosis is excellent.

s1-91.ref: Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery
w: Correct. A direct hernia passes through Hesselbach's triangle.
An indirect hernia passes through the deep ring.
A femoral hernia passes through the femoral canal.
An obturator hernia passes through the obturator canal.
steps: Use the inferior epigastric vessels as the landmark.
Medial to them = direct.
Lateral to them = indirect.
Hesselbach's triangle lies medially.
s1-91.mn: 'MDs don't LIe': Medial Direct, Lateral Indirect.

s1-92.ref: Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery; ATLS
w: Correct. In a stable patient, CECT abdomen is the investigation of choice.
FAST is for unstable patients.
DPL is largely replaced by FAST and CT.
Plain X-ray has little value in blunt trauma.
steps: Check haemodynamics first.
Unstable: FAST at bedside.
Stable: CT gives full detail.
CT guides non-operative care.

s1-93.ref: Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery
w: Correct. Posterior openings curve to the posterior midline.
Radial straight tracks apply to anterior openings.
An anterior opening is not expected for a posterior external opening.
Fistulas have an internal opening.
steps: Draw a transverse line through the anus.
Posterior external opening: curved track.
It opens internally at the posterior midline.
Anterior openings go straight.

s1-94.ref: Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery; ATLS
w: Correct. Withdrawal from pain scores M4.
M5 is localising to pain.
M3 is abnormal (decorticate) flexion.
M2 is extension (decerebrate).
steps: Withdrawal is a normal flexion response.
Localising (reaching the stimulus) is one better: 5.
Abnormal flexion is worse: 3.
So withdrawal = 4.

s1-95.ref: Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery
w: Correct. Suspected torsion needs immediate scrotal exploration.
Antibiotics treat epididymitis, not torsion.
Waiting for Doppler loses salvage time.
Elevation and analgesia alone are inadequate.
steps: Teenager with acute scrotal pain = torsion until proven otherwise.
High testis + absent cremasteric reflex support it.
Time is testis: do not delay for imaging.
Explore, detort, fix both sides.

s1-96.ref: DC Dutta's Textbook of Obstetrics; FOGSI/WHO guidance
w: Correct. Magnesium sulphate is the drug of choice for eclamptic seizures.
Diazepam is less effective.
Phenytoin is less effective.
Labetalol controls blood pressure, not seizures.
steps: Eclampsia = seizures in pre-eclampsia.
MgSO4 prevents recurrent seizures best.
Monitor reflexes, breathing and urine output.
Calcium gluconate reverses toxicity.

s1-97.ref: DC Dutta's Textbook of Obstetrics; WHO PPH recommendations
w: Correct. Uterine atony causes most primary PPH.
Genital tract trauma is the second most common cause.
Retained tissue is a less common cause.
Coagulation disorders are least common.
steps: Use the 4 Ts framework.
Tone (atony) is by far the commonest.
Prevent it with active management of the third stage.
Tranexamic acid within 3 hours saves lives.

w: Correct. Fetal heart rate is not part of the Bishop score.
Cervical dilatation is a component.
Station of the head is a component.
Cervical consistency is a component.
steps: The Bishop score assesses the cervix and head.
Five components, all about cervix or station.
Fetal heart rate is not one of them.
A score ≥8 is favourable for induction.
s1-98.mn: Bishop components: 'Call PEDS' = Consistency, Position, Effacement, Dilatation, Station.

w: Correct. Pregnancy tests detect hCG (beta subunit).
hPL is a placental hormone but not tested for pregnancy diagnosis.
Progesterone is not a diagnostic test for pregnancy.
Estriol is a marker in prenatal screening.
steps: Urine pregnancy tests look for beta-hCG.
hCG is made by the syncytiotrophoblast.
It rises rapidly, doubling every ~48 hours.
It peaks at 8-10 weeks.

s1-100.ref: Rotterdam ESHRE/ASRM consensus 2003; International PCOS guideline 2023
w: Correct. Two of three Rotterdam criteria are required.
All three are not required.
One feature is not enough.
Raised LH is not part of Rotterdam criteria.
steps: Rotterdam criteria have three features.
Any two are enough.
Exclude other causes first.
Letrozole is first-line for ovulation induction.

s1-101.ref: Shaw's Textbook of Gynaecology; WHO Medical Eligibility Criteria
w: Correct. CuT 380A is approved for 10 years.
3 years is too short.
5 years applies to Cu 375 and some LNG-IUS.
1 year is incorrect.
steps: Remember device by duration.
CuT 380A: 10 years.
Cu 375: 5 years.
The copper IUD is also the most effective emergency contraceptive.

w: Correct. The ampulla is the commonest site of ectopic pregnancy.
The isthmus is second; it ruptures earlier.
Ovarian ectopic is rare.
Cervical ectopic is rare.
steps: Fallopian tube is the site in most ectopics.
Within the tube, the ampulla is commonest.
Isthmic ectopics rupture earlier.
Treat medically or surgically by stability.

s1-103.ref: Shaw's Textbook of Gynaecology; WHO cervical cancer screening guideline
w: Correct. HPV 16 and 18 cause about 70% of cervical cancers.
HPV 6 and 11 cause genital warts.
HPV 1 and 2 cause common skin warts.
31 and 33 are high-risk but less common than 16 and 18.
steps: High-risk HPV types drive cervical cancer.
16 and 18 are the main culprits.
E6 and E7 inactivate tumour suppressors.
Vaccinate before sexual debut.
